### Health Planning and Management

**Learning Objectives:**

- Describe the steps of the health planning cycle
- Explain the criteria used for setting health priorities
- Distinguish monitoring from evaluation within the planning cycle
- Trace the role of India's Five-Year Plans in health sector development, and the transition to NITI Aayog
- List Gulick's seven POSDCORB management functions
- Apply the planning cycle to a national health programme example
- Describe India's health financing mix and the AB PM-JAY scheme

## Lecture 1: Health Planning Concept and Cycle {background-color="#E6EEF5"}

📚 **Lecture 1 of 7** · **CM16.L1**

*Health planning - concept and the planning cycle*

---

## The Health Planning Cycle {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

A standard sequence used to plan any health programme or policy:

1. **Situation analysis** — collect and interpret data on the population,
   morbidity/mortality, disease distribution, existing facilities and
   manpower, and community attitudes and beliefs
2. **Establishing objectives and goals**
3. **Assessing available resources**
4. **Fixing priorities**
5. **Writing up the formulated plan**
6. **Programming and implementation** — translating policy into annual
   operational plans
7. **Monitoring** — ongoing tracking, enabling timely correction
8. **Evaluation** — assessing whether objectives were achieved
   (efficiency, acceptance, adequacy)

**Note the direct parallel to Chapter 3's descriptive epidemiology** —
situation analysis is essentially applying the person/place/time
framework at the planning stage.

---

## Setting Health Priorities {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

With finite resources, not every identified problem can be addressed at
once. Standard criteria for prioritization include:

- **Burden of disease** (DALYs — Chapter 21)
- **Equity** — impact on the most disadvantaged groups (Chapter 23's
  social determinants lens)
- **Feasibility** — technical and political practicality of intervening
- **Cost-effectiveness** — health gain per unit of resource spent

This is the planning-level application of Rose's population vs. high-risk
strategy trade-off from Chapter 7 — priority-setting decides *which*
problems get a population-wide response at all.

---

## Monitoring vs. Evaluation {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

The planning cycle's last two steps are often confused, but ask
different questions and happen on different timescales:

| | Monitoring | Evaluation |
|---|---|---|
| **Question asked** | "Are we doing what we planned?" | "Did it work?" |
| **Timing** | Continuous, throughout implementation | Periodic — mid-term or at completion |
| **Purpose** | Track process indicators, enable timely correction | Judge outcomes against objectives (efficiency, acceptance, adequacy) |
| **Example** | Tracking monthly ASHA home-visit counts against target | Assessing whether IMR actually fell in the target districts |

**Why the distinction matters:** a programme can pass every monitoring
checkpoint (activities completed on schedule) and still fail evaluation
(no measurable health outcome improved) — process fidelity is not the
same as impact.

---

## Applying the Cycle: A Worked Example {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

Consider NSCAEM (Chapter 15): **situation analysis** established the
disproportionate tribal-population sickle cell burden; **priority
setting** targeted it specifically because of its concentrated, genetic,
identifiable nature; **implementation** rolled out mass screening;
**monitoring** tracks screening numbers against the 7-crore target; final
**evaluation** will assess progress toward the 2047 elimination goal.
Every named national programme in this curriculum has moved through
these same planning-cycle stages, whether or not it's stated explicitly.

*Management methods based on behavioural sciences*

## POSDCORB: Core Management Functions {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Luther Gulick's classic 1937 framework, describing the seven universal
functions of any executive/manager — directly applicable to running a
health programme or facility:

- **P**lanning
- **O**rganizing
- **S**taffing
- **D**irecting
- **CO**ordinating
- **R**eporting
- **B**udgeting

**Why it's still taught:** it gives a simple, complete checklist for
"what does managing a health programme actually involve" beyond just
clinical or technical content — the same operational lens this chapter
applies to Chapters 11–15's programme content.

---

## Management Span of Control {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

Gulick and Urwick, alongside POSDCORB, also argued for a limited
**"span of control"** — recommending roughly 3–6 subordinates per
manager for effective coordination — a principle still referenced in
designing supervisory structures for large-scale health programmes with
many frontline workers (e.g. ASHA supervision structures under NHM).

## Lecture 3: PERT, CPM, and Cost Analysis {background-color="#E6EEF5"}

📚 **Lecture 3 of 7** · **CM16.L3**

*Quantitative management techniques - PERT / CPM, cost analyses,
systems analysis*

---

## PERT and CPM: Scheduling Complex Programmes {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

Once a programme moves from POSDCORB's broad functions to actually
scheduling a multi-step rollout (e.g. building and staffing a new
health facility), two network-based project-management techniques help
plan the timeline:

- **PERT (Programme Evaluation and Review Technique)** — used when
  activity durations are **uncertain**; estimates each activity's time
  using optimistic, most-likely, and pessimistic estimates, useful for
  novel programmes without historical timing data
- **CPM (Critical Path Method)** — used when activity durations are
  **known/fixed**; identifies the **critical path** — the sequence of
  dependent activities with the longest total duration, which
  determines the minimum possible time to complete the whole project,
  since delaying any activity on it delays the entire programme

**Why this matters operationally:** both techniques identify which
activities have no slack (must start/finish on schedule) versus which
have float (can slip without delaying the programme) — turning
"planning" and "implementation" from the cycle above into an actual,
manageable schedule.

**Cost and systems analysis:** alongside PERT/CPM, planners use
**cost-effectiveness/cost-benefit analysis** (health gain per rupee
spent — the same logic behind the priority-setting criteria above) and
**systems analysis** (modelling a programme as interacting inputs,
processes, and outputs to find bottlenecks before they occur).

## Lecture 5: Five-Year Plans, NITI Aayog, and NHP 2017 {background-color="#E6EEF5"}

📚 **Lecture 5 of 7** · **CM16.L5**

*Five-year plans, NITI Aayog and the National Health Policy 2017*

---

## India's Five-Year Plans and Health {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

India ran **twelve Five-Year Plans (1951–2017)**, formulated by the
**Planning Commission** (established 1950, chaired by the Prime
Minister), each setting specific economic and social development
targets — including health-sector allocations for infrastructure,
disease control, and human resources.

- **1969** — the **Gadgil formula** introduced transparent, criteria-
  based resource allocation to states
- **2015** — the Planning Commission was replaced by **NITI Aayog**
  (National Institution for Transforming India), which since the 12th
  Plan's completion (2017) has taken over health-sector planning and
  programming with a more **flexible, non-five-year framework**

---

## From Five-Year Plans to Flexible Governance {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

The shift from fixed Five-Year Plans to NITI Aayog's more continuous,
flexible planning approach reflects a broader governance trend also seen
in global health policy — the same broad movement from the MDGs' fixed,
time-bound targets to the SDGs' more integrated, continuously monitored
agenda (Chapter 12).

---

## Lecture 6: Health Economics, Financing, and AB PM-JAY {background-color="#E6EEF5"}

📚 **Lecture 6 of 7** · **CM16.L6**

*Health economics and health financing; AB PM-JAY*

---

## Health Economics and Financing {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

**Health economics** applies economic principles (scarcity, opportunity
cost, cost-effectiveness) to health-sector decisions — the discipline
underlying the priority-setting criteria covered earlier in this
chapter.

**India's health financing mix:**

- **Out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE)** — historically the dominant
  source of health spending in India, a major driver of
  catastrophic health expenditure and impoverishment
- **General taxation** — funds the public health system (Sub-Centres
  through tertiary hospitals) and centrally sponsored schemes
- **Social/health insurance** — organized-sector schemes (ESI, Chapter
  19) plus publicly funded insurance for the wider population

**Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY)** —
the world's largest publicly funded health insurance scheme, providing
health cover of ₹5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary
hospitalization to India's poorest and most vulnerable ~40% of
families — the second pillar of Ayushman Bharat, alongside the Health
and Wellness Centres/Ayushman Arogya Mandir pillar (Chapter 25).

---

## Health Systems Building Blocks {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

WHO describes six interacting "building blocks" that any functioning
health system's planning must account for: **service delivery,
health workforce, health information systems, access to essential
medicines, financing, and leadership/governance**. Weakness in any one
block — e.g. a health workforce shortage in tribal areas (Chapter 15) —
limits the effectiveness of planning and management improvements made
elsewhere.

---

## Lecture 7: Health Management Information Systems {background-color="#E6EEF5"}

📚 **Lecture 7 of 7** · **CM16.L7**

*Health management information systems - HMIS, RCH portal, Nikshay,
IHIP and ABDM*

---

## Health Management Information Systems {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

The "health information systems" building block above is delivered
in practice through several named digital platforms, each serving a
different data need:

- **HMIS (Health Management Information System)** — the umbrella
  facility-level reporting portal capturing service-delivery data
  (OPD/IPD numbers, programme indicators) from Sub-Centres upward,
  feeding district- and state-level planning
- **RCH Portal** — tracks reproductive and child health service
  delivery (antenatal registrations, institutional deliveries,
  immunization) at the individual beneficiary level
- **Ni-kshay** — the case-based digital surveillance and treatment-
  tracking platform for tuberculosis under NTEP (Chapter 6)
- **IHIP (Integrated Health Information Platform)** — the disease
  surveillance platform covered in Chapter 6's outbreak-investigation
  content, feeding near-real-time outbreak data
- **ABDM (Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission)** — issues every citizen a
  unique digital health ID and interoperable health records, the
  broader digital-health architecture these programme-specific
  platforms increasingly plug into

**Why these are taught as a set:** each solves a different piece of
the same underlying problem — a functioning health system needs
facility-level, programme-specific, and patient-level data flowing
upward simultaneously, not just one of the three.
